s0001: Find the move between two places on a grid named with letters and numbers
s0002: First compare the letters to find how many squares to move right or left. Then compare the numbers to find how many squares to move up or down.
s0003:
Aziz is playing on a game board. His counter is on square B6.
Which move takes the counter to square F4?
s0008: B → F: B, C, D, E, F — 4 squares right
s0009: We count from B to F: C, D, E, F — four squares to the right.
s0011: We go down from six to four — two squares down.
s0012: Answer: A) 4 squares right and 2 squares down
s0013: So the correct answer is A.
s0014: A student who chose B swapped the number of moves to the right and down.
s0015: A student who chose C forgot that the numbers increase from bottom to top: going from 6 to 4 is moving down.
s0016: A student who chose D mixed up right and left.
s0017: The letters increase to the right, and the numbers increase upward.

Malika is playing on a game board. Her counter is on square G2.
Which move takes the counter to square C5?
s0023: G → C: F, E, D, C — 4 squares left
s0024: We count from G to C: F, E, D, C — four squares to the left.
s0026: We go up from two to five — three squares up.
s0027: Answer: B) 4 squares left and 3 squares up
s0028: So the correct answer is B.
s0029: A student who chose A swapped the number of moves to the left and up.
s0030: A student who chose C mixed up left and right.
s0031: A student who chose D mixed up up and down: going from 2 to 5 is moving up.
s0032: Compare the letters first, then the numbers.
s0033: Recognize a line of symmetry of a shape
s0034: Imagine folding the shape along the dashed line. If the two halves land exactly on top of each other, the line is a line of symmetry.
s0035: In which shape is the dashed line a line of symmetry?
s0036: Line of symmetry: when folded, the two halves land on top of each other
s0037: If we fold along a line of symmetry, the two halves cover each other exactly.
s0038: A: diagonal of a rectangle — halves do not match
s0039: If we fold a rectangle along a diagonal, the corners do not land in the same place.
s0040: C and D: the two parts are different
s0041: In C the line is not in the middle, and in D the two parts have different shapes.
s0042: B: isosceles triangle — the two halves are the same
s0043: In B the line divides the triangle into two identical halves.
s0046: A student who chose A thought the diagonal was a line of symmetry because it divides the shape into two equal parts, but when folded the parts do not land on top of each other.
s0047: A student who chose C chose it because of the vertical line, but the line does not go through the middle of the square.
s0048: A student who chose D thought the line from the vertex was a line of symmetry, but the sides of the triangle are not equal.
s0049: Imagine folding the shape along the line: do the two halves land on top of each other?
s0050: Nilufar cut four shapes out of paper and drew a dashed line on each. In which shape is the dashed line a line of symmetry?
s0051: Line of symmetry: the two halves land on top of each other
s0052: We imagine folding each shape along the line.
s0053: A: rhombus, line through the midpoints of two sides — halves do not match
s0054: If we fold A, the slanted sides do not match each other.
s0055: B: diagonal of a rectangle; D: parallelogram — halves do not match
s0056: In B and D, too, the two halves do not cover each other.
s0057: C: isosceles trapezoid — left and right halves are the same
s0058: In C the vertical line divides the trapezoid into two identical halves.
s0061: A student who chose A thought the line was a line of symmetry because it divides the shape into two equal parts.
s0062: A student who chose B thought the diagonal was a line of symmetry.
s0063: A student who chose D thought the middle line of the parallelogram was a line of symmetry, but when folded the corners do not match.
s0064: Is the part on one side of the line the mirror image of the part on the other side?
s0065: Read values from a bar graph and find the difference between them
s0066: Read from the scale the number each bar reaches (pay attention to the in-between lines), then subtract the smaller from the larger.
s0067:
The bar graph shows the number of ice creams sold in a shop in one day.
How many more strawberry ice creams were sold than vanilla ones?
s0081: We subtract eight from twenty: twelve.
s0083: Twelve more strawberry ice creams were sold.
s0084: A student who chose A compared strawberry with chocolate: $20 - 14 = 6$.
s0085: A student who chose B only read the number of vanilla ice creams.
s0086: A student who chose C only read the number of strawberry ice creams and did not subtract.
s0087: Find the number each of the two bars reaches and compare them.
s0088:
The bar graph shows the number of books in the class library.
How many more fairy tale books are there than poetry books?
s0098: The fairy tales bar reaches sixteen.
s0100: The poetry bar reaches the six line.
s0101: We subtract six from sixteen: ten.
s0103: There are ten more fairy tale books.
s0104: A student who chose A compared the fairy tales with the adventure books: $16 - 12 = 4$.
s0105: A student who chose B only read the number of poetry books.
s0106: A student who chose D only read the number of fairy tale books and did not subtract.
s0107: Follow the end of each bar down to the scale at the bottom.
